newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Most New Zealand CEOs see stable economic policy.
newsitem.headline: Most New Zealand CEOs see stable economic policy.

text.p: New Zealand's business community expects no significant changes to current economic policy after the October 12 general election but this is largely predicated on a win for the conservative government, according to a survey by Ernst and Young and the National Business Review.
More than 60 percent of the 795 business policymakers who responded expected a coalition led by the conservative National Party to win the election.
More than half expected a fall in interest rates and over a third expect a drop in inflation. Most see a flat economy for the balance of 1996 but a strengthening in 1997, Ernst and Young said.
A drop in the exchange rate is expected by 46.7 percent, while 43.3 percent see higher sales and 46.3 percent see customer demand increasing.
Fifty-eight percent believed the central Reserve Bank should continue under its current guidlines, but 36 percent said they should be broader.

"The positive view of 1997 is somewhat surprising given that New Zealand is about to experience its first MMP election," Ernst and Young Chief Executive John Judge said in reference to the new system of proportional representation.
"In the run-up to previous elections, when the political mix has been much less volatile, there has been some uncertainty accompanied by a freeze on investment."
MMP, or Mixed Member Proportional, is set to produce a minority or coalition government, a novelty for New Zealand.

The survey was taken in early September. Recent opinion polls suggest the outcome is too close to call but the opposition Labour, economic nationalist New Zealand First and left-wing Alliance parties may be capable of ousting National if they can agree terms for a coalition.
Judge said respondents expected lower profitability over the next quarter. Sixty-one percent saw no change in pricing, while 43 percent expected margins to tighten.
